nodes.subject: anti-reflective optical coating
nodes.object: less reflection can improve transmission and image contrast while performance changes with wavelength and incident angle

support_spans.exact_quote: An anti-reflective ( AR ), anti-glare or anti-reflection coating is a type of optical coating applied to the surface of lenses , other optical elements, and photovoltaic cells to reduce reflection .
This makes the structure's performance change with wavelength and incident angle , so that color effects often appear at oblique angles .

accepted_phrases: Anti-reflective coatings can reduce reflection and stray light, improving transmission and contrast, while performance depends on wavelength and angle. The mechanism does not establish which exact seller lens has the best coating or a visible output advantage.

nodes.subject: prime lens category
nodes.object: a prime is less versatile than a zoom and is often, but not automatically, faster, lighter or optically superior

support_spans.exact_quote: In film and photography, a prime lens is a fixed focal length photographic lens (as opposed to a zoom lens ), typically with a maximum aperture from f2.8 to f1.2.
While a prime lens of a given focal length is less versatile than a zoom lens, it is often of superior optical quality, wider maximum aperture, lighter weight, and smaller size.

accepted_phrases: A photographic prime is a fixed-focal-length lens; compared with a zoom it is less versatile and is often faster, lighter, smaller or optically better. Often is not always, and the category statement does not rank the exact 35mm, 40mm, 50mm and zoom offers.

nodes.subject: photographic lens design
nodes.object: light capture, color, evenness, sharpness, flare, aberrations, weight, cost and mechanical operation are traded against sensor and use limits

support_spans.exact_quote: The design of photographic lenses for use in still or cine cameras is intended to produce a lens that yields the most acceptable rendition of the subject being photographed within a range of constraints that include cost, weight and materials.
photographic lenses are not always designed for maximum possible resolution since the recording medium would not be able to record the level of detail that the lens could resolve.

accepted_phrases: Photographic lens design balances acceptable rendition against cost, weight, materials, flare, aberrations and mechanical behavior, and maximum possible resolution may exceed the recording medium's needs. This rejects a one-dimensional price-to-sharpness cutoff.

nodes.subject: chromatic aberration
nodes.object: dispersion can produce color fringes, with axial and transverse forms behaving differently

support_spans.exact_quote: In optics , chromatic aberration ( CA ), also called chromatic distortion , color aberration , color fringing , or purple fringing , is a failure of a lens to focus all colors to the same point.
Chromatic aberration manifests itself as "fringes" of color along boundaries that separate dark and bright parts of the image.

accepted_phrases: Chromatic aberration occurs when colors do not share one focus or magnification and can appear as colored fringes at contrast boundaries. It must be measured by position, aperture and output rather than inferred from price or a product label.

nodes.subject: spherical aberration
nodes.object: the effect can be stronger at short focal ratios and can be corrected with optical design choices

support_spans.exact_quote: Light rays that strike a spherical surface off-centre are refracted or reflected more or less than those that strike close to the centre. This deviation reduces the quality of images produced by optical systems.

The effect is proportional to the fourth power of the diameter and inversely proportional to the third power of the focal length, so it is much more pronounced at short focal ratios , i.e., "fast" lenses.

accepted_phrases: Spherical aberration can make central and outer rays focus differently and may be more pronounced at fast focal ratios, while design can correct it. A wider f-number alone therefore neither guarantees nor disproves sharp output.

nodes.subject: lens flare
nodes.object: bright sources, optical interfaces and shading affect visible artifacts and contrast loss

support_spans.exact_quote: A lens flare is a visual artifact caused by light scattering , or flaring, in a lens system.
The glare makes the image look "washed out" by reducing contrast and color saturation

accepted_phrases: Lens flare comes from scattering or internal reflection and can create visible artifacts or washed-out contrast, especially with bright sources. It must be tested with declared light position and hood use, not inferred from element count, coating copy or price.

nodes.subject: optical transfer function
nodes.object: contrast transfer varies with spatial frequency, focus and the full imaging chain

support_spans.exact_quote: The optical transfer function ( OTF ) of an optical system such as a camera , microscope , human eye , or projector is a scale-dependent description of their imaging contrast.
This derived function is commonly referred to as the modulation transfer function ( MTF ).

accepted_phrases: OTF, and its commonly used magnitude MTF, describes how imaging contrast changes with spatial scale. It is not one context-free sharpness score and must be tied to focus, sensor, processing, display or print size and relevant detail.

nodes.subject: diffraction limit
nodes.object: smaller apertures increase diffraction and at f/22 many modern lenses can be diffraction limited

support_spans.exact_quote: any optical instrument or system â a microscope , telescope , or camera â has a principal limit to its resolution due to the physics of diffraction .
At small apertures, such as f/22 , most modern lenses are limited only by diffraction and not by aberrations or other imperfections in the construction.

accepted_phrases: Diffraction sets a physical resolution limit and grows as the aperture is made smaller; at f/22 many modern lenses can be diffraction limited. Stopping down can reduce some aberrations yet eventually reduce detail, so aperture tests need the intended output.
